summary: Deprioritize. The strategy comes from Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang (2004), who sort stocks each month on idiosyncratic volatility relative to the Fama-French three-factor model and find that the lowest-volatility quintile outperforms the highest. We tested the long-only, equal-weighted lowest-volatility quintile on a 415-name S&P 500 survivor universe over 2015 to 2025 and found net CAGR of 11.92% against 12.71% for the equal-weight universe, with Sharpe 0.63 against 0.65. The Monte Carlo fund simulation put the probability of positive NPV at 34%, with a median incremental fee PV of -$600k against the equal-weight universe fund. The edge fails at 10 bps, holds in neither sub-period, and the group ranking runs the wrong way, so the recommendation is to deprioritize even though implementation reliability is green.

sections.What the paper proposes: The paper tests whether stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility, measured as the standard deviation of residuals from a daily regression on the Fama-French market, size and value factors over the past month, earn different returns. It reports that they earn low returns: the difference in FF-3 alphas between quintile 5 and quintile 1 is -1.31% per month, with a t-statistic of -7.00, and the raw 5-1 average return difference is -1.06% per month. The selected experiment is Table VI, Panel B, value-weighted quintile portfolios in the 1/0/1 strategy (one month of formation, no skip, one month of holding), rebalanced monthly. The authors call the pattern a puzzle, because it runs opposite to theories that predict a positive idiosyncratic volatility premium and because exposure to aggregate volatility risk explains very little of it.
sections.What we implemented and changed: We computed the signal as residual volatility from a one-month window of daily returns on the three Fama-French factors, formed quintiles each month, and held the lowest-volatility quintile for one month with no skip. The paper's sample runs July 1963 to December 2000. Ours runs 2015-01-01 to 2025-12-31 on a 415-name survivor universe of today's S&P 500 constituents, with 19 names excluded for missing data. We made six adaptations: equal weighting instead of value weighting, a long-only favored group with no short leg, equal-count breakpoints over eligible names, our own universe and sample period, and market capitalization not used. Three fields were assumed because the paper is silent: no price floor, a minimum of 252 days of history, and a minimum of 15 trading days in a formation month. Eight details were left open by the paper and run on engine defaults, including whether regressions use excess or raw returns, delisting treatment, and the source of the daily factors. Costs are 10 bps, and execution is at the first trading-day close of the following month.
sections.What the backtest found: The strategy did not beat the equal-weight universe. Net CAGR was 11.92% against 12.71% for the equal-weight universe and 0.13453 for SPY; gross CAGR was 0.13603. Net Sharpe was 0.63 against 0.65 for the equal-weight universe. Net maximum drawdown was -0.378297. The four-factor alpha t-statistic was -0.10, so there is no measurable alpha after costs. At 0 bps the alpha t-statistic is 0.834021, and at 25 bps it is -1.5008, so the result depends on costs. Both sub-periods fail to beat the equal-weight universe. The ranking of the five volatility groups does not match the paper: the highest-volatility group, group 5, had the highest mean monthly return of 0.011596, above group 1 at 0.010337, and the rank correlation of 0.70 is not in the expected direction. The paper's sign did not reproduce in this sample.
sections.What the simulation and economics found: We simulated a fund with 2/20 fees and a 5% hard hurdle by bootstrapping historical days in blocks, and measured incremental fees against an equal-weight universe fund charged the same schedule. The fraction of paths with positive NPV is 0.345, and the median incremental fee PV is -599526.0, roughly -$600k. The strategy ended ahead of SPY in only 0.041 of paths and ahead of the equal-weight fund in 0.373. When the historical mean excess return is removed, the fraction with positive NPV is 0.522, which is what noise alone would produce, so the simulation shows no edge beyond chance. Break-even AUM is not defined because expected incremental fees are negative. The fee schedule is an assumption for a long-only fund, not an observed one, and the bootstrap cannot create regimes absent from the sample. Annual costs were about 0.015019 of average portfolio value, with mean monthly turnover of 0.626888.
sections.How reliable the interpretation was: Implementation reliability is green: 3 fields were assumed, 6 adapted, evidence was valid for 100% of material fields, and there were 0 critical check disagreements. Extraction ran once, so run-to-run agreement is not informative. Scoring against the reference is preliminary. Agreement with the preliminary reference was 0.769231, with one critical mismatch on the signal formula wording, where the reference allows a market-model residual and ours uses the three-factor residual, and minor mismatches on required inputs and the headline result. Limitations are the survivor universe, which flatters returns, equal weighting where the paper uses value weights, the long-only adaptation, a sample that lies entirely after publication, zero yield on cash, Yahoo adjusted-close conventions, and an assumed fee schedule. Effort reduction from the engine was not measured.
sections.What to do next: Do not allocate further research time to this strategy as specified. If the idea is revisited, the first step is to remove the survivor bias with a point-in-time universe including delisted names, and to test value weighting and a long-short version closer to the paper before concluding that the effect is absent after publication. Any revisit should also set the open items, such as excess versus raw returns and the factor source, explicitly, and confirm against the final reference once the preliminary reference is replaced.
